analysis.one_liner: Requires warning labels on food packaging containing the chemical BPA.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Health Committee when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Department of Health and Human Services to complete a safety assessment of bisphenol A (BPA), a chemical used in food can linings and packaging, focusing on low-dose exposure and vulnerable groups like pregnant women and infants. It would then require any food in BPA-containing packaging to carry a label saying the packaging contains BPA, an endocrine-disrupting chemical. States would remain free to adopt stricter rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who want to know whether the cans, jars, and plastic containers they buy contain BPA, a chemical the National Institutes of Health has linked to endocrine disruption. Pregnant women, infants, children, the elderly, and workers exposed to BPA on the job would get a full government safety assessment that must account for them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food shoppers, especially pregnant women and families

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends federal food law to prohibit selling food in BPA-containing packaging unless the label states: "This food packaging contains BPA, an endocrine-disrupting chemical, according to the National Institutes of Health."

It requires HHS to issue a revised safety assessment for BPA food containers within 180 days of enactment, considering low-dose exposure and vulnerable populations, and to decide whether there is reasonable certainty of no harm.
It includes a savings provision preserving the right of states, localities, and Indian tribes to adopt or enforce stricter BPA rules or warnings.

analysis.who_pays: Food and beverage companies whose canned and packaged goods use BPA-based linings, and chemical suppliers that produce the resin, would bear the cost of labeling and possibly of reformulating products. Consumers might see slightly higher packaging costs passed through, though many alternatives already exist.

drawbacks.text: Critics of mandatory labeling could argue that regulators have repeatedly judged typical BPA exposure safe, and that a federal warning label on nearly all canned food could confuse shoppers more than it informs them, since it does not tell them the level of exposure or whether the amount matters.

The bill's label language embeds a fixed scientific characterization in statute, so it would not update even if future research changed the scientific picture; and relabeling or reformulating food packaging imposes real costs on manufacturers that could partly reach consumers through prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to shoppers is modest per purchase but broad in reach: a clear, truthful label on packaging containing a contested chemical, plus a safety review required to weigh vulnerable groups. The cost falls on a narrow industry and is likely small relative to the reformulation many companies were already beginning. The bill is a transparency measure, not a ban, so it leaves businesses free to choose BPA-free alternatives or keep using BPA with disclosure.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Dianne Feinstein introduced S. 821, the BPA in Food Packaging Right to Know Act, on March 19, 2015, joined by Sen. Patrick Leahy and one other cosponsor.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where it stayed for the rest of the 114th Congress.
The full action history shows no committee business, no reported bill, and no floor action after the referral; the Congress ended January 3, 2017 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food and packaging manufacturers that use BPA-based linings, and the chemical suppliers behind them, are better off: they avoided a mandatory disclosure label and a new federal safety assessment without ever having to argue against the bill on the floor. Shoppers who would have used the label remain without the information it would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: BPA packaging makers and chemical suppliers

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it referred to the Senate Health Committee.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only three sponsors, all Democrats or independents; no one spoke or voted against it, because it never advanced far enough for opponents to engage.

industries.note: BPA-based epoxy linings are standard in most food cans, so nearly all canned goods would have needed the warning label unless the packaging changed. The industry's interest in avoiding the label runs directly against shoppers' interest in knowing what their packaging contains.

industries.industry: Chemical producers of BPA and epoxy resins
industries.note: A required HHS safety assessment weighing low-dose effects and vulnerable groups, plus public labeling of the chemical, would put the product's safety record under new scrutiny and could shrink demand. A cheaper, unexamined status quo is what these suppliers keep when a bill like this dies in committee.

industries.industry: BPA-free packaging and can-lining alternatives makers
industries.note: A disclosure requirement would push food companies toward alternative linings and plastics, creating demand for substitutes. That interest coincides with consumers' ability to avoid BPA.
